title: Coiled rope rug
subtitle: Thick cotton rope coiled and joined in double crochet
excerpt: A 50 cm round rug made from thick cotton rope coiled in a flat spiral and joined with double crochet stitches through the rope. No yarn: works with 5 mm cotton macramé rope. Advanced due to the tension needed to keep the coil flat.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Coiled rope rugs crocheted through thick cord are a domestic tradition that predates standardised crochet; this version uses readily available cotton macramé cord.

crochet.gaugeText: Work with 5 mm cotton macramé rope on a 10 mm hook. Each coil round adds approx. 4, 5 cm to the diameter. 6 rounds gives approx. 50, 55 cm.
crochet.finishedSizeText: Approx. 50, 55 cm diameter. Add extra coil rounds for a larger rug.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat-coil technique for rugs and baskets. The working cord is held alongside the previous coil and joined by crocheting through both at regular intervals to form a firm flat disc.

content.text: A coiled rope rug is a 50 cm disc worked by
coiling construction

, 5 mm cotton macramé rope is coiled in a flat spiral, and each new coil is joined to the previous one with double crochet stitches worked through both strands. No yarn is needed, only the rope itself. The 10 mm hook is the right size for piercing through two strands of 5 mm rope. The result is firm, washable, and reversible.

items.label: Large-eye tapestry needle (for burying rope ends)

content.text: Materials
Approx. 60 m of 5 mm single-twist or braided cotton macramé rope. One 100 m spool with some left over.
Gauge
Work with 5 mm cotton macramé rope on a 10 mm hook. Each coil round adds approx. 4, 5 cm to the diameter. 6 rounds gives approx. 50, 55 cm.
Stitches used
Slip stitch (sl st). Used to join the start of each coil round
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc). Worked through both the new coil and the previous coil simultaneously.
Pattern

Centre ring: coil the rope end into a tight circle about 5 cm across (approximately 3, 4 wraps). Using the hook, work dc stitches through both layers of the coil all the way around, pulling firmly to close the centre. Sl st to join (approx. 8, 10 dc).

Coil round 2: continue the rope spiral, laying the new coil against the outside of round 1. Work dc stitches through both the new coil and the previous round, spacing them approx. Every 2, 3 cm. Work 2 dc into the same spot approx. Every 5th join to keep the coil lying flat. Sl st at end of round to join.

Rounds 3, 6: continue the spiral, joining the new coil to the previous one with evenly-spaced dc stitches. Add extra dc joins at any point where the coil starts to cup upward (every 4th join rather than every 5th). After 6 rounds, the rug should be approx. 50 cm diameter.
Finishing the end: cut the rope at a point that completes the round evenly. Thread the cut end through a large tapestry needle and bury it back through the previous coil for at least 5 cm to secure.

Work on a hard flat surface and regularly press the rug down as you go: gravity and a firm surface are your main flatness tools here. If the rug cups, undo back to the previous round and add more dc joins on the outside edge.
Finishing

Bury the rope tail through the last coil using the tapestry needle. No weaving-in. The tail is hidden inside the rope structure. Wet the rug lightly and press flat under heavy books for 30 minutes if it needs final shaping.
Care
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. Cotton macramé rope can loosen slightly with washing: press flat again after the first few washes.
